script.problem: It reuses a line from the Prep cards word for word.
It has 2 sentences. Explanations are 3 to 5 sentences.

terra.problem: The claim that Egypt appears in plenty of Bible stories is a Bible fact without a reference.
The claim that Edom is a land in the Bible has no reference.
The passage does not say Naomi had been waiting for this news.
The text says the LORD provided food, not that the famine had ended.
Saying the sons haven't grown up yet makes hypothetical sons sound as though they already exist.
The verse says they wept aloud again, but does not specify that all three women were weeping.
The quotation joins Naomi's words across the intervening 'said Naomi' without showing the omission, and changes the punctuation after 'Look.'
The quote 'wherever you go, I will go.' changes the comma after 'go' to a period and does not show that the sentence continues.
The women's question does not establish that they know exactly who Naomi is.
The quotation ends 'Call me Mara' with a period, but the BSB has a comma and continues Naomi's sentence.
The quotation 'Call me Mara.' changes the BSB's comma after 'Mara' to a period and omits the continuation.

explanations.explanation: Moab is right. A famine hits the land, and a man from Bethlehem in Judah takes his wife and two sons to reside in the land of Moab (Ruth 1:1). Think about that move. I got carried across one kitchen into a drawer and I needed a whole angel to sort me out, and this family relocates to a different country.

Egypt shows up in plenty of Bible stories, but it isn't this one. The text says the man went to reside in the land of Moab (Ruth 1:1). Hold onto Moab, because it's going to matter for this whole story.

Edom is a real land in the Bible, but it's not where this family goes. Ruth 1:1 says the man went to reside in the land of Moab, with his wife and his two sons. Moab is the name to remember. It's all over this passage.
Ruth it is! The text says the sons took Moabite women as their wives, one named Orpah and the other named Ruth (Ruth 1:4). Put that name in your pocket, baker. She walks through this whole story.

Rachel isn't a name in this passage. Ruth 1:4 says the sons took Moabite women as their wives, one named Orpah and the other named Ruth. I know, a lot of R names are flying around. Orpah and Ruth are the two to watch.
Dinah doesn't show up in this story. The text names the two Moabite women as Orpah and Ruth (Ruth 1:4). Say them both out loud once, and they'll stick.

Yes. After they had lived in Moab about ten years, both Mahlon and Chilion died, and Naomi was left without her two sons and without her husband (Ruth 1:5). I think this one hurts, friend. It's a heavy part of her story, so let's give it a quiet moment.

explanations.answer: Her house in Moab burns down
explanations.explanation: The text says nothing about a fire or a house. What it says is that both Mahlon and Chilion died (Ruth 1:5). It's a heavy verse, and I think it hurts to read. Naomi was left without her two sons and without her husband.

explanations.answer: She falls sick and loses her sight
explanations.explanation: Nothing in this passage says Naomi gets sick or loses her sight. Ruth 1:5 says that both Mahlon and Chilion died, and Naomi was left without her two sons and without her husband. It's a heavy verse, so let's go gently.

Food! Naomi heard in Moab that the LORD had attended to His people by providing them with food (Ruth 1:6). Remember the famine back in verse 1? That's the news she's been waiting on. Food news is my favorite news. I run a bakery.
No king in this verse. Naomi heard in Moab that the LORD had attended to His people by providing them with food (Ruth 1:6). A famine is where this story began, so the news is that the food is back.

There's no battle in this verse, so no victory either. The news Naomi hears in Moab is that the LORD had attended to His people by providing them with food (Ruth 1:6). This one is about the famine ending. It's a quieter kind of good news.

explanations.answer: Go back to their mothers' homes
explanations.explanation: That's it. Naomi tells them, “Go back, each of you to your mother’s home.” (Ruth 1:8). They're on the road to Judah with her, and she turns around and points them back. That's a surprise, and the story is just getting started.

explanations.answer: Walk faster to beat the dark
explanations.explanation: Naomi never says a word about the pace or the dark. She tells them, “Go back, each of you to your mother’s home.” (Ruth 1:8). So no speed walking in this passage. It's a turnaround on the road.

explanations.answer: Stay close to her the whole way
explanations.explanation: It's the opposite. Naomi says, “Go back, each of you to your mother’s home.” (Ruth 1:8). They set out with her on the road to Judah, and here she's sending them home. Keep that in mind, because it sets up what comes next.
True. Naomi says, “May the LORD enable each of you to find rest in the home of your new husband.” (Ruth 1:9). That's a blessing for both of them. Then she kisses them, and the tears start.

It's actually true. Naomi says, “May the LORD enable each of you to find rest in the home of your new husband.” (Ruth 1:9). It's right there in her send-off. She's speaking a blessing over both women before the goodbye.

explanations.answer: We will return with you to your people
explanations.explanation: Right. They say, “Surely we will return with you to your people.” (Ruth 1:10). Naomi just told them to go home, and they answer by saying they'll go with her. Two women, one very firm "no thanks."

explanations.answer: We will stay in Moab and wait for you
explanations.explanation: That's not what they say. The text says they answered, “Surely we will return with you to your people.” (Ruth 1:10). Nobody offers to wait in Moab. They want to go with her.

explanations.answer: We will come visit you in Bethlehem
explanations.explanation: No visit is mentioned here. Orpah and Ruth say, “Surely we will return with you to your people.” (Ruth 1:10). That's more than a visit. They're saying they'll go with Naomi.

explanations.answer: Would you wait for them to grow up
explanations.explanation: Yes. Naomi asks, “would you wait for them to grow up?” (Ruth 1:13). She goes on, “Would you refrain from having husbands?” Naomi is working through her case one question at a time, and she's not rushing.

explanations.answer: Would you raise them as your own
explanations.explanation: Naomi never asks that. Her question is, “would you wait for them to grow up?” (Ruth 1:13). It comes with a second one: “Would you refrain from having husbands?” Raising anyone isn't in her words.

explanations.answer: Would you go ahead to Bethlehem
explanations.explanation: Naomi doesn't ask them to go ahead of her. She asks, “would you wait for them to grow up?” (Ruth 1:13). Bethlehem isn't in this part of her speech. She's talking about sons who haven't grown up yet.

explanations.answer: The LORD's hand has turned against her
explanations.explanation: That's what Naomi says. She tells them, “it is much more bitter for me than for you, because the hand of the LORD has gone out against me.” (Ruth 1:13). I think she's carrying a lot right now, friend. These are her words, and the story is still going.

explanations.answer: The people of Judah have turned against her
explanations.explanation: Naomi never says that about Judah. Her words are, “it is much more bitter for me than for you, because the hand of the LORD has gone out against me.” (Ruth 1:13). The people of Judah aren't mentioned in this speech. She talks about the LORD's hand.

explanations.answer: The people of Moab have turned against her
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that about Moab. Naomi says, “it is much more bitter for me than for you, because the hand of the LORD has gone out against me.” (Ruth 1:13). Those are her words in the passage. She doesn't point at the people around her.

True. Ruth 1:14 says that Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye. They had all been weeping aloud again, and Orpah says her goodbye. That's one daughter-in-law's choice, and the other one chooses differently.

It's actually true. The text says, “Again they wept aloud, and Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye…” (Ruth 1:14). Orpah is the one who says goodbye with a kiss. Ruth does something different in the same verse.
Not this time. Ruth 1:14 says Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye, “but Ruth clung to her.” Ruth doesn't go home with Orpah. She holds on to Naomi.
False is right. Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye, “but Ruth clung to her.” (Ruth 1:14). So Ruth stays with Naomi instead of going home. That's a big choice, and her next speech is even bigger.

True. Naomi says, “Look, your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and her gods; follow her back home.” (Ruth 1:15). She says it right to Ruth's face, and Ruth is still standing there. I'd say Ruth is about to change the mood.

It's actually true. Naomi tells Ruth, “your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and her gods; follow her back home.” (Ruth 1:15). That's a direct word to Ruth. It sets up her answer in the next verse.

explanations.answer: Naomi's God will be her God
explanations.explanation: Yes. Ruth says, “your people will be my people, and your God will be my God.” (Ruth 1:16). Those words are part of one promise. Her whole answer is about going where Naomi goes.

explanations.answer: She will take care of Naomi's house
explanations.explanation: That's not in Ruth's promise. She says, “your people will be my people, and your God will be my God.” (Ruth 1:16). A house isn't mentioned. Her words are about going with Naomi and about Naomi's people and God.

explanations.answer: She will learn all the ways of Judah
explanations.explanation: Ruth doesn't say that. Her words are, “your people will be my people, and your God will be my God.” (Ruth 1:16). She doesn't list ways to learn. She promises to go with Naomi, and Naomi's God will be her God.

Death. Ruth says, “May the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, if anything but death separates you and me.” (Ruth 1:17). That's a promise with no exit door in it. Only one thing could pull these two apart.
Distance isn't the word. Ruth says, “if anything but death separates you and me.” (Ruth 1:17). She has already said, “wherever you go, I will go.” That promise isn't about how far away anyone is.

Marriage isn't what Ruth says. Her words are, “May the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, if anything but death separates you and me.” (Ruth 1:17). Only death is on her list. Nothing else gets a spot.

explanations.answer: She stops trying to persuade her
explanations.explanation: That's what she does. The text says, “When Naomi saw that Ruth was determined to go with her, she stopped trying to persuade her.” (Ruth 1:18). The arguing is over. Ruth said her piece, and it was enough.

explanations.answer: She sends her back after Orpah
explanations.explanation: Naomi did say that back in Ruth 1:15, but it's not what she does now. After Ruth's promise, Naomi saw that Ruth was determined to go with her, and she stopped trying to persuade her (Ruth 1:18). So no more sending. The two of them go on together.

explanations.answer: She tells her to wait in Moab
explanations.explanation: The text never has Naomi say that. Ruth 1:18 says she saw that Ruth was determined to go with her, and she stopped trying to persuade her. No waiting in Moab is on the table. They head for Bethlehem together.

Yes. When they entered Bethlehem, the whole town was stirred, and the women of the town exclaimed, “Can this be Naomi?” (Ruth 1:19). They say her name out loud. Naomi doesn't answer with a quick "hi, it's me."
That's not what the women say. They exclaim, “Can this be Naomi?” (Ruth 1:19). They ask about her by name. Her husband isn't mentioned in their words.
The women don't call anyone a stranger. The text says they exclaimed, “Can this be Naomi?” (Ruth 1:19). They use her name. They seem to know exactly who she is.

Mara. Naomi says, “Do not call me Naomi… Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me.” (Ruth 1:20). She gives the women a new name to use. It's a heavy moment, so we'll stay with her in it.
Hannah isn't a name in this passage. Naomi says, “Do not call me Naomi… Call me Mara.” (Ruth 1:20). Mara is the name she gives. Hannah isn't part of the scene.
Leah doesn't appear here. Naomi tells the women, “Do not call me Naomi,” and then, “Call me Mara.” (Ruth 1:20). Mara is the name she asks for. That's the one to hold onto.

It's flipped. Naomi says, “I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty.” (Ruth 1:21). She's not saying full on the way back. These are her own words about how she sees it, and I think they hurt.

False is right. Naomi says, “I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty.” (Ruth 1:21). She went away full and came back empty. It's her own telling, and I think she carries a lot in that sentence.

Barley! Naomi and Ruth arrived in Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest (Ruth 1:22). Remember the news back in Moab, that the LORD had provided food for His people (Ruth 1:6)? Now the barley's coming in, and the two women walk right into it.

Wheat is a good guess, but the text says barley. They arrived in Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest (Ruth 1:22). That's the harvest that's starting as they walk in. Hang onto it, because it's going to matter.
Olives aren't in this verse. Ruth 1:22 says they arrived in Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest. Barley is the crop in this verse. It's the harvest coming in as the two women arrive.
